title: Chinese Literature
description: Dream of the Red Chamber, Lu Xun, contemporary novelists

concepts.title: Classical Chinese Poetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinese literature has the longest continuous literary history of any tradition. The classical poetry of the Tang dynasty (618-907) — Li Bai (701-762), Du Fu (712-770), Wang Wei (701-761), Bai Juyi (772-846) — is the central canon.

Tang poetry's distinctive features: short lyric forms (typically 4 or 8 lines), strict tonal patterning, parallelism, allusive density, classical literary Chinese grammatically distinct from the spoken language.

Du Fu is widely considered the greatest Chinese poet — a Confucian humanist whose poems on war, exile, family, and historical decline have continuing moral weight. Li Bai is the wilder Daoist counterpart — wine, the moon, immortals, the imagination's flight.

The translation challenge is immense. English translations from Pound's Cathay (1915) onward have shaped Anglo-American poetry's image of China.

concepts.title: The Classical Novels
concepts.contentHtml:
Imperial China produced four canonical great novels:

Romance of the Three Kingdoms (Luo Guanzhong, 14th century) — historical epic of the late Han collapse.

Water Margin (Shi Nai'an, 14th century) — bandit-heroes during the Song dynasty.

Journey to the West (Wu Cheng'en, 16th century) — the monk Tripitaka and his companions (most famously the Monkey King) travelling to India for Buddhist scriptures.

Dream of the Red Chamber (Cao Xueqin, 18th century) — the decline of an aristocratic family. The most psychologically and aesthetically refined of the four; for many readers the greatest Chinese novel.

All four remain foundational to Chinese popular culture — adapted endlessly in film, television, opera, video games.

concepts.title: Lu Xun and the May Fourth Generation
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern Chinese literature dates from the May Fourth Movement of 1919 — a cultural and political reform movement that broke with classical literary Chinese in favour of the vernacular (baihua).

Lu Xun (1881-1936) is the central figure. His short stories — 'Diary of a Madman' (1918, the first major work in vernacular Chinese), 'A Madman's Diary,' 'The True Story of Ah Q' (1921), 'Medicine,' 'Hometown,' 'Kong Yiji' — anatomise traditional Chinese society's failures with savage precision.

Other May Fourth writers: Lao She (Rickshaw Boy, 1936), Mao Dun, Ba Jin, the poet Xu Zhimo, the dramatist Cao Yu.

concepts.title: Mao Era and After
concepts.contentHtml:
The Maoist period (1949-1976) was hostile to most kinds of literature. Socialist realism was the only sanctioned mode; traditional and modernist work was suppressed; major writers (Lao She among them) died during the Cultural Revolution.

The post-Mao reform era (1978-) brought a literary renaissance. Scar literature processed the Cultural Revolution's traumas. Root-seeking literature looked back to traditional Chinese sources. The Misty Poets (Bei Dao, Shu Ting, Gu Cheng) revived modernist lyric.

Major contemporary novelists: Mo Yan (Nobel 2012, Red Sorghum, Life and Death Are Wearing Me Out), Yu Hua (To Live, Brothers), Wang Anyi, Yan Lianke, Liu Cixin (The Three-Body Problem, science fiction).

concepts.title: Sinophone Literature
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinese-language literature is not confined to mainland China. Sinophone writing includes Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, the diaspora.

Taiwan: Eileen Chang (Zhang Ailing, 1920-1995, perhaps the major 20th-century Chinese writer of fiction); Pai Hsien-yung; Wu He; Wu Ming-yi.

Hong Kong: Xi Xi, Liu Yichang, Dung Kai-cheung.

The diaspora: Ha Jin (writes in English), Yiyun Li (English), Yan Geling, Gao Xingjian (Nobel 2000, France-based, writes in Chinese).

The political pressures on mainland literature have made Sinophone writing outside mainland China increasingly important. Some of the most ambitious contemporary writing in Chinese is being produced in Taipei, Hong Kong, and the diaspora.

concepts.title: The Tale of Genji
concepts.contentHtml:
The Tale of Genji (Genji monogatari), composed by Murasaki Shikibu around 1010, is widely considered the world's first novel. A 54-chapter narrative of court life centred on Prince Genji's many love affairs.

Murasaki was a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court. The novel registers in extraordinary detail the aesthetic and emotional life of that aristocracy — the cultivation of taste, the codes of poetry exchange, the protocols of secret romance, the mood of mono no aware (the pathos of impermanence).

The book was lost in part for centuries; the standard text is reconstructed. English translations: Arthur Waley (1925-33, freer), Edward Seidensticker (1976), Royall Tyler (2001), Dennis Washburn (2015).

concepts.title: Heian Court Literature
concepts.contentHtml:
The Heian period (794-1185) was Japanese literature's first golden age. Court women — barred from learning Chinese, the language of official prose — wrote extraordinary works in vernacular Japanese.

Sei Shōnagon's The Pillow Book (c. 1002) is a collection of observations, lists, anecdotes, opinions. Witty, sharp, snobbish, sometimes savage. Roland Barthes among others has used it as a model for the fragmentary essay.

Murasaki's Genji and her own diary; Izumi Shikibu's diary and poetry; the anonymous Kagerō Diary; the poetic anthology Kokin Wakashū (905) — the period's prose and poetry remain central reference points.

concepts.title: Bashō and Haiku
concepts.contentHtml:
Matsuo Bashō (1644-1694) is the central figure of the haiku tradition.

The haiku is a 17-syllable (5-7-5) verse form, conventionally on a seasonal subject, conventionally pivoting on a single observation. Bashō refined it from earlier comic verse forms into a major literary mode.

His travel narratives, especially The Narrow Road to the Deep North (Oku no Hosomichi, 1702), combine prose journals with embedded haiku. The mode — haibun — is itself a major form.

Other major haiku poets: Buson (1716-1784), painter as well as poet; Issa (1763-1827), more colloquial and tender; Masaoka Shiki (1867-1902), the modernising reformer.

concepts.title: Modern Japanese Fiction
concepts.contentHtml:
The Meiji Restoration (1868) opened Japan to Western influence; modern Japanese literature followed.

Natsume Sōseki (1867-1916) is the central modern Japanese novelist. I Am a Cat (1905-06), Botchan (1906), Kokoro (1914), Sanshirō (1908). Sōseki's portraits of modern Japanese consciousness — its struggles between Western individualism and traditional social structure — set the form for 20th-century Japanese fiction.

Other major figures: Tanizaki Jun'ichirō (The Makioka Sisters, 1948), Akutagawa Ryūnosuke ('In a Grove,' 'Rashōmon'), Kawabata Yasunari (Nobel 1968, Snow Country), Mishima Yukio, Ōe Kenzaburō (Nobel 1994).

concepts.title: Contemporary Japan
concepts.contentHtml:
Murakami Haruki (b. 1949) is now Japan's most internationally known writer. Norwegian Wood (1987), The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle (1994-95), Kafka on the Shore (2002), 1Q84 (2009-10).

Murakami's mode: dreamlike realism, jazz and Western literary references, alienated male protagonists, missing women, parallel worlds. His relationship to the Japanese literary tradition is debated — his style is unusually Anglophone.

Other contemporary novelists: Murakami Ryū (no relation), Yoshimoto Banana, Ogawa Yōko, Kawakami Mieko, Yū Miri.

Japanese genre fiction — particularly mystery, literary horror, and graphic narrative (manga) — has international reach. Higashino Keigo's mysteries; Suzuki Kōji's horror (Ring, 1991).

title: Arabic & Persian Literatures
description: Thousand and One Nights, Rumi, Hafez, Mahfouz

concepts.title: Classical Arabic Poetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry — the Mu'allaqāt, the 'suspended odes' of the late 6th and early 7th centuries — established Arabic verse forms that would last a millennium.

The classical Arabic qaṣīda is a long monorhymed ode in strict quantitative metres. Its conventional sections — desert lament, journey, praise of patron — became models for Islamic-era poetry.

Major classical poets: Imru' al-Qays (pre-Islamic), Abu Nuwas (8th-9th century, the great wine and love poet of Abbasid Baghdad), Al-Mutanabbi (10th century, considered by many the greatest Arabic poet), Al-Ma'arri (11th century, philosophical and pessimistic).

concepts.title: The Thousand and One Nights
concepts.contentHtml:
One Thousand and One Nights (Alf Layla wa-Layla) is the most internationally famous work of Arabic literature. The frame: Scheherazade tells stories nightly to delay her execution by King Shahryar.

The collection accumulated over centuries from Indian, Persian, Arabic, and other sources. The earliest manuscripts date to the 14th century; later additions continued through the 18th. Some of the most famous tales (Aladdin, Ali Baba, Sinbad) entered through 18th-century French translation.

The Nights's influence on world literature has been incalculable. Borges, García Márquez, Salman Rushdie, A. S. Byatt, Naguib Mahfouz all work in dialogue with it.

concepts.title: Persian Poetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical Persian poetry produced four canonical figures.

Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (Book of Kings, c. 1010) is the Persian national epic — 50,000+ couplets covering Iranian history from creation through the Arab conquest.

Rumi (1207-1273) is the central mystical poet. The Masnavi — six books of teaching couplets — and the Divan of lyrics in honour of his master Shams. The most-translated Persian poet in English; also extensively misrepresented in Anglophone popular versions.

Hafez (c. 1320-1389) is the master of the lyric ghazal. Wine, love, divine love, the wine that may be either wine or divine love. Goethe's West-östlicher Divan is in dialogue with him.

Saadi's Gulistan and Bustan (13th century) are foundational works of Persian prose-and-verse moral teaching.

concepts.title: Modern Arabic Literature
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern Arabic literature emerged in the 19th and 20th centuries, particularly in Egypt and Lebanon, partly in response to European literary forms.

Naguib Mahfouz (1911-2006) is the central figure. Egyptian, Nobel Prize 1988. The Cairo Trilogy (1956-57) — three novels following a single Cairo family across the early 20th century — is his major work. Children of the Alley (1959) was banned in much of the Arab world for its allegorical handling of religious figures.

Other major novelists: Tayeb Salih (Sudan, Season of Migration to the North, 1966), Ghassan Kanafani (Palestine, Men in the Sun), Hanan al-Shaykh, Elias Khoury, Alaa Al Aswany, Hoda Barakat.

concepts.title: Modern Persian and Arabic Poetry
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern Persian poetry: Nima Yushij (1897-1960) initiated free verse in Persian; Forugh Farrokhzad (1934-1967), the major modern woman poet; Ahmad Shamlou; Sohrab Sepehri.

Modern Arabic poetry: the Shi'r magazine (Beirut, 1957-1970) was central to modernist Arabic poetry; Adonis (Ali Ahmad Said Esber, b. 1930), Syrian-Lebanese, the major contemporary Arabic poet; Mahmoud Darwish (1941-2008), the central Palestinian voice; Nizar Qabbani; Nazik al-Mala'ika.

The relationship between Arabic and Persian literatures has been continuous since the 7th-century Arab conquest of Persia. Persian writers wrote in Arabic; Arabic literary forms were absorbed into Persian. The bilingual literary culture of medieval and early modern West Asia shaped both traditions.

title: African Literatures
description: Achebe, Soyinka, Adichie, Coetzee — voices of a continent

concepts.title: Oral Traditions
concepts.contentHtml:
African literatures' deepest roots are oral. Across the continent, traditions of griots (West African praise-singer historians), epic recitation, oral poetry, riddle, folktale, and proverb have carried literary forms for centuries before written records.

The Mali epic Sundiata — composed in Mande and transmitted orally for some 800 years — is the most famous African oral epic. The Mwindo Epic from the Congo, the Ozidi Saga from the Niger Delta, the Akan Anansi tales — all are major oral literary works.

Modern African writers — Soyinka, Achebe, Ngũgĩ, the négritude poets — have drawn on these traditions in writing, both formally and as implicit cultural reference.

concepts.title: Achebe and African Anglophone Fiction
concepts.contentHtml:
Chinua Achebe (1930-2013) is widely considered the founding figure of modern African anglophone fiction. Things Fall Apart (1958) is the central work — the story of Okonkwo, an Igbo wrestler and warrior, and the disruption of Igbo society by British colonialism.

The novel was deliberately written as an answer to European colonial fiction (Conrad, Cary, Greene) that had presented Africans as backdrop. Achebe insisted that pre-colonial Igbo society was complex, articulate, internally contested, fully human — and that colonialism's violence required understanding before judgment.

Achebe's other novels: No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964), A Man of the People (1966), Anthills of the Savannah (1987). His essay 'An Image of Africa' (1975) on Conrad's Heart of Darkness reshaped postcolonial criticism.

concepts.title: Anglophone West and East Africa
concepts.contentHtml:
Wole Soyinka (b. 1934, Nigeria, Nobel 1986) is a major dramatist, poet, novelist, and essayist. Death and the King's Horseman (1975) is his most-performed play.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o (b. 1938, Kenya) wrote the early novels in English (Weep Not, Child, A Grain of Wheat) before switching to Gikuyu — arguing that African literature in colonial languages perpetuates colonial mentalities. Decolonising the Mind (1986) is the central essay.

Other major figures: Ben Okri (The Famished Road, 1991), Buchi Emecheta, Ama Ata Aidoo, Nuruddin Farah, Tsitsi Dangarembga, Yvonne Vera.

concepts.title: Francophone and Lusophone Africa
concepts.contentHtml:
Négritude — the 1930s francophone Caribbean and African literary movement — established a tradition. Léopold Sédar Senghor (Senegal, later first President), Aimé Césaire (Martinique), Léon Damas (French Guiana) were the founding figures.

Major francophone African writers: Mongo Beti (Cameroon), Sembène Ousmane (Senegal, also a major filmmaker), Ahmadou Kourouma (Côte d'Ivoire), Mariama Bâ (So Long a Letter, 1980), Boubacar Boris Diop, Alain Mabanckou.

Lusophone African literature: Pepetela and José Eduardo Agualusa from Angola; Mia Couto from Mozambique. Couto's prose, mixing Portuguese with Bantu-language idioms, is among the most distinctive in contemporary world fiction.

concepts.title: South Africa and the New Generation
concepts.contentHtml:
South African literature has a distinct trajectory shaped by apartheid (1948-1994).

Nadine Gordimer (1923-2014, Nobel 1991), J. M. Coetzee (b. 1940, Nobel 2003), Athol Fugard (drama), Alan Paton (Cry, the Beloved Country, 1948) wrote under and through the apartheid system. Coetzee's Disgrace (1999) and the earlier Waiting for the Barbarians are his major novels.

The new generation of African writers — many writing for international audiences, often based partly outside Africa — includes Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (Half of a Yellow Sun, 2006; Americanah, 2013), Teju Cole, Helon Habila, Yaa Gyasi, NoViolet Bulawayo, Tsitsi Dangarembga, Imbolo Mbue, Maaza Mengiste, Abdulrazak Gurnah (Nobel 2021).

title: Latin American Literature
description: Beyond the Boom — Bolaño, Lispector, regional traditions

concepts.title: Pre-Boom Foundations
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin American literature did not begin with the 1960s Boom. Earlier traditions established essential ground.

Rubén Darío (Nicaragua, 1867-1916) led the modernismo movement — the late 19th-century Spanish-American renewal of poetry that influenced Spain itself.

Pablo Neruda (Chile, 1904-1973, Nobel 1971), César Vallejo (Peru, 1892-1938), Gabriela Mistral (Chile, 1889-1957, Nobel 1945), Octavio Paz (Mexico, 1914-1998, Nobel 1990) are the major 20th-century Spanish-language poets.

Pre-Boom prose: Jorge Luis Borges (Argentina, 1899-1986), Juan Rulfo (Mexico, Pedro Páramo, 1955 — a foundational magical-realist text before the term existed), Alejo Carpentier (Cuba), Miguel Ángel Asturias (Guatemala, Nobel 1967).

concepts.title: The Boom
concepts.contentHtml:
The Latin American Boom of the 1960s and 1970s brought Spanish-American fiction to international attention. Four central figures.

Gabriel García Márquez (Colombia, 1927-2014, Nobel 1982): One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), Love in the Time of Cholera (1985), Chronicle of a Death Foretold (1981).

Mario Vargas Llosa (Peru, 1936-2025, Nobel 2010): The Time of the Hero (1963), Conversation in the Cathedral (1969), The Feast of the Goat (2000).

Julio Cortázar (Argentina, 1914-1984): Hopscotch (1963), the short fictions Blow-Up.

Carlos Fuentes (Mexico, 1928-2012): The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962), Terra Nostra (1975).

concepts.title: Lispector and Brazilian Fiction
concepts.contentHtml:
Brazilian literature is its own tradition — Portuguese-language, often distinct from Spanish-American currents.

Machado de Assis (1839-1908) is the founding modern Brazilian novelist. Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (1881), Dom Casmurro (1899). Susan Sontag and Harold Bloom have championed him as a great underappreciated novelist; recent translations have widened his Anglophone readership.

João Guimarães Rosa (1908-1967): The Devil to Pay in the Backlands (1956), one of the great untranslatable novels — its sertão Portuguese resists English. Jorge Amado reached wide international audiences. Lygia Fagundes Telles.

Clarice Lispector (1920-1977) is now widely considered the central Brazilian writer of the 20th century. Novels (The Passion According to G.H., The Hour of the Star) and short fiction (Family Ties) — interior, philosophical, formally radical.

concepts.title: Post-Boom and Contemporary
concepts.contentHtml:
Latin American writers after the Boom have largely worked in resistance to its mode.

Roberto Bolaño (Chile, 1953-2003) is the central post-Boom figure. The Savage Detectives (1998), the posthumous 2666 (2004). His work is metafictional, sceptical of the Boom's totalising ambitions, attentive to violence and failure.

Other major contemporary figures: Mario Bellatín, Alejandro Zambra (Chile), Valeria Luiselli (Mexico), Samanta Schweblin (Argentina), Mariana Enriquez (Argentina), Pola Oloixarac, Yuri Herrera, Fernanda Melchor, Lina Meruane, Carmen María Machado.

Argentina's literary scene — built on Borges, Cortázar, Bioy Casares — remains particularly productive. Buenos Aires sustains one of the world's densest contemporary literary cultures.

concepts.title: Caribbean and Other Regional Traditions
concepts.contentHtml:
The Caribbean has its own traditions — Spanish, French, English, Dutch, creole languages.

Aimé Césaire (Martinique), Édouard Glissant (Martinique), Maryse Condé (Guadeloupe), Patrick Chamoiseau (Martinique) — francophone and creole writing.

Derek Walcott (Saint Lucia, Nobel 1992): Omeros (1990), the major Caribbean epic. V. S. Naipaul (Trinidad, Nobel 2001), Jamaica Kincaid, Edwidge Danticat (Haiti), Marlon James (Jamaica).

Cuban literature has its own distinct trajectory through and after the 1959 Revolution: Alejo Carpentier, José Lezama Lima, Reinaldo Arenas, Leonardo Padura.

Each Latin American country has its own literary tradition. The 'Latin American literature' shorthand obscures real internal differences. The continent's literary production is among the world's most vital.
